name: Soviet Chic
summary: This article is about the Soviet-inspired aesthetics seen in the new wave, post-punk, and EBM/industrial scenes in the 1980s-1990s.
description:
This article is about the Soviet-inspired aesthetics seen in the new wave, post-punk, and EBM/industrial scenes in the 1980s-1990s. Not to be confused with Communist Chic .

Soviet Chic refers to the use of Soviet iconography, Constructivist graphic design, and Eastern Bloc military dress within Western New Wave , Post-Punk , and Electronic Body Music (EBM) scenes of the 1980s and into the 1990s. Unlike the later, depoliticized Communist Chic , which applies hammer-and-sickle imagery and faux Cyrillic as decontextualized consumer decoration, Soviet Chic as documented here emerged from underground music scenes and the fashion press as a direct engagement with Cold War politics, drawing on genuine Soviet aesthetics to comment on the ideological standoff between East and West rather than to strip it of meaning. The term itself was in period use; a 1989 cover of the Los Angeles Times Magazine read " Soviet Chic: From High Fashion to High Finance—Suddenly All Things Russian Are Red Hot ," describing the trend as it was happening. [ 1 ]
culturalContext: Key values (per the Aesthetics Wiki): Cold War irony, East-West juxtaposition, anti-Thatcherism and anti-Reaganism, political satire
